source.title: Cannabidiol in Anxiety and Sleep: A Large Case Series

authoritative_validator_execution.mode: exact supplied source files copied byte-for-byte into temporary import package

anchor_support_checks.excerpt: This study aimed to determine whether CBD is helpful for improving sleep and/ or anxiety in a clinical population. Given the novel nature of this treatment, our study also focused on tolerability and safety concerns.
A retrospective chart review was conducted of adult psychiatric patients treated with CBD for anxiety or sleep as an adjunct to treatment as usual at a large psychiatric outpatient clinic.
Selection for the case series was contingent on informed consent to be treated with CBD for 1 of these 2 disorders and at least 1 month of active treatment with CBD.
Patients with sole or primary diagnoses of schizophrenia, posttraumatic stress disorder, and agitated depression were excluded.
The sampling frame consisted of 103 adult patients who were consecutively treated with CBD at our psychiatric outpatient clinic.

The final sample consisted of 72 adult patients presenting with primary concerns of anxiety (65.3%; n = 47) or poor sleep (34.7%; n = 25) and who had at least 1 follow-up visit after CBD was prescribed.

Nearly all patients were given CBD 25 mg/d in capsule form. If anxiety complaints predominated, the dosing was every morning, after breakfast. If sleep complaints predominated, the dosing was every evening, after dinner.

The Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale is a widely used and validated anxiety measure with 14 individual questions. It was first used in 1959 and covers a wide range of anxiety-related concerns. The score ranges from 0 to 56.

The Pittsburg Sleep Quality Index is a self-report measure that assesses the quality of sleep during a 1-month period. It consists of 19 items that have been found to be reliable and valid in the assessment of a range of sleep-related problems.
Side effects and tolerability of CBD treatment were assessed through spontaneous patient self-reports and were documented in case records.
Deidentified patient data were evaluated using descriptive statistics and plotted graphically for visual analysis and interpretation of trends.
By the second monthly follow-up, 41 patients (56.9%) remained on CBD treatment and completed assessments;
27 patients (37.5%) remained on CBD treatment at the third monthly assessment.
At the first monthly assessment after the start of CBD treatment, 79.2% (57/72) and 66.7% (48/72) of all patients experienced an improvement in anxiety and sleep, respectively;

Two patients discontinued treatment within the first week because of fatigue.
Three patients noted mild sedation initially that appeared to abate in the first few weeks.
One patient with a developmental disorder (aged 21 years) had to be taken off the CBD regimen because of increased sexually inappropriate behavior.
One patient noted dry eyes.
Four patients declined CBD treatment because of religious or ethical concerns about the relation to cannabis.
These results demonstrated a more sustained response to anxiety than for sleep over time.
These results must be interpreted cautiously because this was a naturalistic study, all patients were receiving open-label treatment, and there was no comparison group.
Most patients were also taking psychiatric medications and receiving other mental health services, such as counseling, which limits the ability to make any causal links to CBD treatment.
the clinical population in this case series is skewed younger than typical for our clinic, and future studies could explore the possible selection bias inherent in this treatment option.
the large societal notoriety about cannabis and medical marijuana probably contributes to a larger-than-normal placebo effect.
Clinical attrition is evident in the dataset. The reason for this might be related to CBD ingestion or not, so the overall component remains unclear.

CBD displays promise as a tool for reducing anxiety in clinical populations, but given the open-label and nonrandomized nature of this large case series, all results must be interpreted very cautiously. Randomized and controlled trials are needed to provide definitive clinical guidance.

CV Sciences Inc, Las Vegas, NV, provided cannabidiol products for the study. CV Sciences was not involved in the data collection, data interpretation, preparation of the report, or decision to submit the report for publication.

Dr Shannon has published several professional books on integrative mental health. Dr Shannon is a Principal Investigator for a Phase 3 study of 3,4-methylenedioxy-methamphetamine (MDMA)-assisted psychotherapy for severe posttraumatic stress disorder and receives compensation for his clinical work from the Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies, Santa Cruz, CA.

semantic_spot_checks.claim: At the first monthly assessment, 57 of 72 patients (79.2%) had improved anxiety after starting CBD.
Table 1 reports a HAM-A mean of 18.02 (SD 7.56) for the primary anxiety group at 1 month.
The study was naturalistic and open-label with no comparison group, so efficacy could not be established from the observed changes.
One 21-year-old patient with a developmental disorder developed increased sexually inappropriate behavior that resolved when CBD was held and recurred after rechallenge; CBD was then discontinued.

The authors concluded that CBD showed promise for reducing anxiety but emphasized that the open-label, nonrandomized case series required very cautious interpretation and that randomized controlled trials were needed for definitive guidance.
